Senses.Note: Baiyun Du asks Wujian Xiandu about the hidden intent of the ancestral arrival. Wujian answers, 'When Mount Sala nods, I will tell you.' Du gestures as if to answer; Wujian shouts, and Du replies with a verse in which the peak is already full of waves and seasons. Jie'an and Tui'an transmit the encounter and compose separate verses. Gulin answers that saying the place has been found still misses it, while Shanduo asks his listeners whether the mountain has nodded already. The impossible condition turns a request for an explanation into a test of the questioner's response.

Senses.Note: Pang asks who is not companion to the myriad things. Mazu replies that he will tell him once Pang drinks the West River dry in one gulp. Senses.Note: Sansheng asks Xuefeng what a gold-scaled fish that has passed through a net eats. Xuefeng replies, 'Come out of the net, and then I will tell you.' Sansheng rebukes him for failing to recognize the question, and Xuefeng says he has much abbey business. Sanshan treats the exchange as a test on both sides. Yuanwu asks whether the fish has actually escaped; Tianqi responds with a verse of the fish leaping into open water; Wuyi asks again what such a fish eats. Xuefeng's sentence sends the supposed escape back to the questioner instead of supplying an answer about fish food.

SearchAliases: when the stone tortoise can speak, i will tell you
Senses.Note: A monk asks Longya for the meaning of the ancestral arrival. Longya says he will answer when a stone tortoise speaks. The monk claims it has spoken; Longya asks what it said, and the monk has no reply. Pufu offers the monk a substitute question. Linquan reads the exchange alongside Longya’s earlier visits to teachers, while later commentators test whether Longya withheld or displayed the answer. The impossible tortoise turns the monk’s demand back toward his own words.

Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (J/J37/J37nB392.xml). Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Hansong Cao. Plum blossom and snow each yield something to the other: snow is whiter, while plum has fragrance. Hansong Zhicao quotes the full poem after mentioning the woman who supported a hermitage keeper for twenty years and regularly sent a young woman to serve him. He grants that both the woman and the monk have strengths, but says the Buddhist matter remains far away. The poem's opening dispute over spring and its balanced concessions thus acknowledge relative merits without making either party's advantage sufficient. The exact couplet is quoted poetry, not a newly composed reply by Hansong.

Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (J/J38/J38nB433.xml). Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Chunbeide. In an address on the Buddha's awakening, Chunbei Guangde dramatizes Shakyamuni entering the assembly's nostrils and proclaiming that all beings possess a Buddha's wisdom but fail to realize it through delusive attachment. Chunbei calls this making respectable people lowly, shouts, and asks how such speech could emerge if mind, Buddha and beings are without difference. Saying that what is so may resemble the truth but resemblance is not yet it, he closes with plum and snow. The inherited couplet preserves a difference within apparent likeness; it is not merely praise of two attractive winter objects.

During a snow address, a monk asks Lingyin Yinwen about the lion king's roar, then whether it is miraculous power or simply natural functioning. Lingyin answers with the plum-and-snow couplet. Luyan He raises Zhaozhou's reply to a question about the complete round appearance of Vairocana: since becoming a monk young, he has never had blurred vision. Luyan says this avoids harm but has not yet entered the marketplace to help others. Senses.PreferredTarget: the wondrous mind of nirvana
Senses.Explanation: One member of the flower-sermon transmission formula, paired with “the treasury of the true teaching eye” (正法眼藏). In The Gateless Barrier, Śākyamuni Buddha says that he has the true-eye treasury and the wondrous mind of nirvana and entrusts them to Mahākāśyapa. Zhongfeng Mingben groups the phrase with names such as awakening, nirvana, true thusness, wisdom, and the true-eye treasury, then says that “all are established from this mind; the names always differ while their substance is always the same” (一依此心建立。名常異而體常同). Zhe'an Jingfan contrasts clever talk about the treasury with deep thought about this wondrous mind; Tianru Weize repeatedly questions what could be called by either name. In these uses “wondrous mind” (妙心) is explicitly a mind, wondrous or subtle; it is not a “secret essence.”

Senses.Explanation: ‘The mind of nirvana is easy to grasp; discerning wisdom is hard to clarify’ warns against stopping at a broad claim of insight. These masters turn the line toward particular cases, people, and acts that still require clear response. Yuanwu places the line among images for exact master-student response, then asks what Mazu's shout did. Miyun links it to Sudhana's many visits and offers his staff as a guide. Guting uses it in the wild-fox case to check a shallow understanding of cause and effect. Xueguan cites it to require seeing through many schools and disputed cases. Guxue says a turn back to original insight must be followed by fine conduct among differences. Pinjixiang uses the saying in personal instruction, then says the road remains open despite a traveler's confusion.

Senses.PreferredTarget: Nirvana and birth-and-death are alike empty flowers
SearchAliases: nirvana and birth-and-death are alike empty flowers
Senses.Note: The line compares both nirvana and birth-and-death to flowers seen in empty space. Jifei says it during a memorial reflection on an elderly lay follower, then considers her family. Shenfeng voices it at a monk remembrance and lifts a whisk toward the departed. Miyin gives it after asking how one does not leave the world of appearances. Senses.Explanation: One hall address places “bronze-headed and iron-browed” directly under “the patch-robed monk's gate.” Verses nevertheless say that even such a fellow receives a welt from one staff-blow, or stands bloodied under the staff's command. Elsewhere the phrase itself answers “What is buddha?”, followed by the equally concrete “bird's beak and fish's gills.” These occurrences establish the epithet and its Chan setting; they do not establish literal metal anatomy or an occult quality. The headword occurs 208 times across 114 texts.

Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (J/J26/J26nB178.xml). Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Feiyin. At the close of a retreat, Feiyin Tongrong hears a monk describe a mouth only half opened after years of confinement. He thanks the monk for the retreat's work, says the other half is still unopened, and meets a shout with laughter. His ensuing verse makes straw sandals fierce as tigers and a staff alive as a dragon, then declares that copper-headed, iron-foreheaded men are all on his mountain. A kicked-open barrier and an eight-sided freedom continue the vigorous imagery, but he ends by asking about a bottomless bowl and rejects two monks' answers. The phrase praises toughness and freedom under testing; the failed replies prevent reading it as an unconditional certificate for everyone present.

Occurrences.Kwic: 住順寧府雲州五福禪院語錄據室。驀拈拄杖，云：「隔江望見，撩起便行。好箇阿師！得與麼利？未跨船舷，好與三十棒。好箇阿師！得與麼鈍？新五福者裏要且無利鈍可柬責。何故？銅頭鐵額漢，盡在我山中。」
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (J/J29/J29nB224.xml). Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Yezhu of Mount Song. Taking his seat at Wufu, Yezhu Fuhui raises his staff and evokes someone who sees from across a river and immediately sets out: how sharp! Before the boat's edge is crossed, however, thirty blows would be deserved: how dull! He then says that at the new Wufu there is no sharpness or dullness to pick over, because copper-headed, iron-foreheaded men are all on his mountain. The pair caps this deliberate change of evaluation. It announces a demanding welcome rather than supplying a literal account of metal-headed residents, and does not establish that any particular visitor has already passed his examination.

Occurrences.Kwic: 小參。「十五日已前，滴水冰生；十五日已後，冷灰豆爆；正當十五日，諸方開爐設舖。山僧者裏又且不然，一年三百六十日，日日開爐；一日十二箇時，時時煆煉。且煆煉箇甚麼？銅頭鐵額漢，盡在我山中。」
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (J/J34/J34nB308.xml). Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Xiangya Ting. Xiangya Xingting contrasts the days before and after the fifteenth with freezing water and beans bursting from cold ashes. Other teachers open their furnaces at the midpoint, but his furnace is open every day of the year and the forging continues through every hour. What is being forged? He answers with the copper-headed, iron-foreheaded men all on his mountain. Here the phrase supplies the human product of a sustained training image. The furnace language gives the hardness its local force; it need not imply physical invulnerability or that training has ceased once the boast is spoken.

Occurrences.Kwic: 「如何是三總同參？」師云：「銅頭鐵額漢，盡在我山中。」
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (J/J37/J37nB388.xml). Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Yikui of Shending. During an assembly in the snow, a monk asks Yikui Yuankui about the 'three who study together.' Yikui answers that copper-headed, iron-foreheaded men are all on his mountain. The wider dialogue moves through questions of true wisdom and ordinary bodily, eating and seasonal replies; it does not pause to define a special class of three people. His answer brings the question back to the strong practitioners of this present assembly. The line functions as a forceful response under questioning, while the exact relation of its imagery to the monk's technical phrase remains unstated.
